new_statements.quote: [p. 47] "As a typical Hui Chinese variety, Tunxi Hui has six citation tones and a very complex tone sandhi system." [p. 49] "When tone sandhi happens, it is exclusively the preceding tone in a disyllabic word or phrase that will change its tone value, a pattern known as right-dominant tone sandhi." [p. 54] "Neutral tones in Tunxi Hui, while they may be found, are not as evident or as common as in Mandarin. They only occur in functional words, such as some grammatical words such as the genitive marker and the perfective aspect marker, and sentence final particles, or the second reduplicated verb in a verb phrase."

All three quoted sentences are present verbatim at the stated pages (page = centred number line closing the page): p. 47 (txt l. 2976-2979) 'As a typical Hui Chinese variety, Tunxi Hui has six citation tones and a very complex tone sandhi system.'; p. 49 (l. 3075-3081) rule (i) 'When tone sandhi happens, it is exclusively the preceding tone in a disyllabic word or phrase that will change its tone value, a pattern known as right-dominant tone sandhi.'; p. 54 (l. 3317-3326, section 2.5.3 opening) 'Neutral tones in Tunxi Hui, while they may…
new_statements.relation_note: new: nothing on record. Language not in catalog and no existing statements; this work supplies a first prosodic-type statement (tonal, six tones, right-dominant sandhi, toneless function-word syllables) but no word-stress rule.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Tunxi Hui is described as a lexical-tone language: six citation tones (11, 44, 31, 24, 42, checked 5), extensive right-dominant disyllabic tone sandhi (the first syllable changes, the final syllable keeps its citation tone), and toneless 'neutral-tone' syllables restricted to function words (genitive ka, perfective, sentence-final particles, cliticized weak pronouns, second copy of a reduplicated verb), whose pitch is set by the preceding tone (p. 55). The thesis has no section on word stress and makes no statement about stress placement or its absence; the only uses of 'stress' are 'unstressed weak forms' for cliticized toneless pronouns (p. 125) and 'prosodically prominent' strong pronoun forms a24-le etc. 'in terms of not only volume and length, but also pitch and timbre' (p. 123).
new_statements.exceptions: Neutral (toneless) syllables only in function words and verb reduplicants; 'the neutral tones in Tunxi Hui are not always neutral' - realised approx. as low tone 1 after Tones 11/31/42 and higher tone 3 after Tones 44/24/5 (p. 55, after Qian 1997). Tone 11 splits into two sandhi classes by Middle Chinese origin (p. 48 n. 23).
new_statements.identity_note: The work describes Tunxi Hui 屯溪话 (Xiuyi subgroup of Hui Chinese, Tunxi district of Huangshan city, southern Anhui; ~70,000 speakers), largely following Qian (1997) for the tone system; huiz1242 'Hui Chinese' is the Glottolog language-level node covering all Hui varieties (Jixi, Yixian, Xiuning, Wuyuan etc. are other varieties with files in the same folder).

tone_statements.citation: Zhang, Minghui & Fang Hu. 2015. Tone features in Qimen Hui Chinese Dialect. In: Proceedings of the 18th International Congress of Phonetic Sciences (ICPhS 2015), Glasgow, paper 0192 (5 pp.).
tone_statements.quote: The Qimen Hui Chinese dialect has 6 tonal categories, namely yin-ping, yang-ping, shang, yin-qu, yang-qu and yin-ru. … In summary, Qimen tones are transcribed as follows: yin-ping /22/, yang-ping /55/, shang /41/, yin-qu /23/, yang-qu /33/, and yin-ru /25/. … The shang tone /41/ becomes /44/ or /22/ before or after the yang-ping tone /55/, respectively ([21]). The yin-ru tone /25/ usually becomes a short tone /5/ when occurring in the leftmost position in a sandhi domain. … In summary, Qimen distinguishes three level tones, two rising tones, and one falling tone.
tone_statements.locator: Sec. 1 Introduction; Sec. 3 Results, end; Sec. 4 Discussion and conclusion; paper unpaginated

tone_statements.citation: Coblin, W. South. 2008. Comparative Phonology of the Yánzhōu Dialects. Bulletin of Chinese Linguistics 3(1): 79-143. DOI 10.1163/2405478x-90000048.
tone_statements.quote: Common Yánzhōu has a classic system of eight tones, i.e., píng 平 , shǎng 上, qù 去, and rù 入 tones in upper and lower register. The tonal systems of the three dialects can be briefly described as follows. Chúnān Tones yīnpíng yángpíng shǎngsheng yángqù yīnrù yangrù 1) Traditional yīnqù merges with yīnpíng. 2) Yángpíng and yángqù are beginning to merge among younger speakers. 3) Yīnshǎng and yángshǎng have merged. ... None of the dialects contrast yīnqù 陰去 and yángqù 陽去, with yīnqù being lost everywhere.
tone_statements.locator: Sec. 4 'The Tones of Common Yánzhōu', pp. 134-135; tone lists repeated in Appendix I
tone_statements.summary: Chun'an, Sui'an and Jiande each have six tone categories, different mergers of the eight yin/yang ping-shang-qu-ru classes set up for Common Yanzhou; category names only, no pitch values or shapes.

tone_statements.translation: III. Six citation tones: yinping [tone letter] 11 (exx.), yinshang 32, yangshang 24, yinqu 55, yinru 213, yangru 35 ... (1) The old shang and ru tones each split into yin and yang classes by the voicing of the old initial. (2) Luo Changpei (1936) said Xiuning has 7 tones. The field records also list 7 categories - yinping (incl. yangqu), yangping, yinqu, yinshang, yangshang, yinru, yangru - but only 6 values are actually marked, yangping and yinqu being marked together as 55.

sources.note: Acoustic study (F0, duration, 10 speakers) of the six citation tones of Qimen Hui: yin-ping /22/, yang-ping /55/ (extra-high, often falsetto), shang /41/, yin-qu /23/, yang-qu /33/, yin-ru /25/ = three level, two rising, one falling tone; no duration contrast; notes sandhi: shang 41 > 44 / 22 next to yang-ping 55, yin-ru 25 > short 5 in leftmost sandhi position; argues contour tones decompose into level components and that yin-qu/yin-ru cross registers.
sources.venue: Proceedings of the 18th International Congress of Phonetic Sciences (ICPhS 2015), Glasgow, paper

tone.translation: III. Six citation tones: yinping [tone letter] 11 (exx.), yinshang 32, yangshang 24, yinqu 55, yinru 213, yangru 35 ... (1) The old shang and ru tones each split into yin and yang classes by the voicing of the old initial. (2) Luo Changpei (1936) said Xiuning has 7 tones. The field records also list 7 categories - yinping (incl. yangqu), yangping, yinqu, yinshang, yangshang, yinru, yangru - but only 6 values are actually marked, yangping and yinqu being marked together as 55.
tone.says: Synchronic phonology of 休宁城内 (Xiuning town) speech compiled from the Luo Changpei (1934) / Shao Rongfen (1955-61) field notebooks: 23 initials, 27 finals, six citation tones 阴平 11 (incl. old 阳去), 阴上 32 (short, glottal constriction, cf. Wu Wei 1990), 阳上 24, 阴去 55 (阳平 marked together with it), 阴入 213, 阳入 35; notes Luo 1936 spoke of 7 tones but only 6 values are marked; 13 儿化 (-n) patterns, some with tone change; the print article (方言 2018.2) carries a homophone syllabary with sandhi marked as in…
